beats.headline: Your empty ArrayList allocates zero bytes.
beats.subline: Its initial allocation waits until the very first add call.
beats.narration: Your empty ArrayList starts with zero allocated backing array space. Its first add call forces a ten element array allocation on the heap. Understanding this growth prevents hidden resizes in your applications.

beats.title: ArrayList 1.5x Capacity Growth
beats.subtitle: How OpenJDK resizes backing Object arrays

nodes.label: Empty ArrayList
nodes.detail: Points to shared empty array to save heap space

nodes.label: Array Full (size == cap)
nodes.detail: Triggers grow() method using bitwise right shift

nodes.label: New Object Array
nodes.detail: Copies items via System.arraycopy to capacity 15

beats.narration: On creation, an empty ArrayList points to a shared empty array. When you add the first element, OpenJDK allocates ten slots. When full, it computes old capacity plus half of old capacity, expanding by 1.5x.

beats.title: Unsized vs. Pre-Sized ArrayList

top.label: Default ArrayList

bottom.label: Pre-Sized ArrayList
points: Allocates single backing array up front
Amortized O(1) appends with zero copying

beats.narration: Adding one hundred thousand items to a default list triggers over twenty array allocations and copy cycles. Pre-sizing the list allocates one backing array up front and eliminates resize overhead completely.

beats.title: Internal Bitwise Capacity Growth

steps.explanation: Bitwise right shift by 1 computes 50 percent capacity increase instantly.
Arrays.copyOf delegates to native System.arraycopy for maximum memory performance.

beats.narration: Inside OpenJDK source, the grow method calculates new capacity by adding half the current length using a bitwise right shift. Arrays dot copyOf then delegates to native System dot arraycopy to move reference pointers fast.

beats.title: ArrayList Resizing Mastered
takeaways: ArrayList starts lazy and allocates 10 on first add
Growth factor is 1.5x via bitwise right shift
Pre-size collections when count is known

beats.narration: That is how ArrayList manages contiguous heap memory. Next in Part 2, we compare ArrayList against LinkedList to see why pointer chasing wrecks CPU caches in production.

beats.headline: LinkedList is often 6x slower than ArrayList.
beats.subline: Big-O notation hides the physical impact of CPU cache lines.
beats.narration: LinkedList claims constant time insertion at both ends, but in real benchmark tests it runs six times slower and consumes six times more memory than ArrayList due to CPU cache misses.

beats.title: Memory Footprint per Element

top.label: ArrayList Memory
top.code:
// Contiguous array of 4-byte references
Object[] elementData = new Object[1_000_000];
points: 4 MB array memory for 1 million items
Packed contiguously with minimal header overhead

bottom.label: LinkedList Memory
points: 24 bytes per node wrapper on 64-bit JVM
24 MB total memory for 1 million elements

beats.narration: With compressed object pointers, an ArrayList slot uses four bytes per reference. LinkedList wraps every element in a separate Node object with pointers and headers, using twenty-four bytes per entry.

beats.title: Cache Locality vs Pointer Chasing
beats.subtitle: Why contiguous arrays outperform scattered heap nodes

nodes.label: 64-Byte Cache Line
nodes.detail: CPUs fetch memory in 64-byte blocks from RAM into L1 cache

nodes.label: ArrayList Iteration
nodes.detail: Contiguous slots fit 16 references per line with prefetching

nodes.label: Node Allocation
nodes.detail: LinkedList nodes sit scattered across heap memory addresses

nodes.label: Pointer Chasing
nodes.detail: Dereferencing node.next stalls CPU waiting on memory

beats.narration: CPUs pull memory into sixty-four byte cache lines. Scanning contiguous ArrayList memory lets hardware prefetch incoming items effortlessly. Traversing LinkedList forces the CPU to chase scattered heap pointers, causing frequent cache misses.

beats.title: Replacing LinkedList with ArrayDeque

steps.explanation: LinkedList creates a new double-pointer node object for every queued item.
ArrayDeque uses a resizable circular array with high cache locality and zero node overhead.

beats.narration: If you need a queue or stack with constant time push and pop, use ArrayDeque instead of LinkedList. ArrayDeque relies on a resizable circular array without wrapper objects, saving memory and maximizing CPU cache hits.

beats.title: Hardware Realities Mastered
takeaways: ArrayList uses 4B per slot vs 24B per LinkedList node
Contiguous arrays enable CPU cache line prefetching
Use ArrayDeque for efficient queues and stacks

beats.narration: Hardware mechanics explain why contiguous memory wins. Coming up in Part 3, we dive into HashSet internals and see how mutating set elements creates silent memory leaks.

parts.partTitle: HashSet Internals & The Mutable Key Bug

beats.headline: Mutating an element inside a HashSet permanently leaks memory.
beats.subline: The item stays trapped inside the set, unreachable by contains or remove.
beats.narration: Mutating an object field after placing it in a HashSet will cause contains and remove calls to fail silently, trapping that object inside heap memory permanently.

beats.title: HashSet Backing HashMap Source

steps.explanation: HashSet uses a single static dummy Object called PRESENT as value for all entries.
Set elements reside as keys in an internal HashMap to guarantee uniqueness.

beats.narration: HashSet does not build its own hashing table. Under the hood, it wraps a HashMap and stores your elements as map keys, pairing every single item with a shared static dummy object named PRESENT.

beats.title: The Mutable Element Bug

steps.explanation: Changing name alters tag.hashCode(), pointing lookup to a different bucket index.
HashSet inspects the new hash bucket, missing the original entry completely.

beats.narration: When you mutate a field participating in hashCode, the computed hash code changes. Future contains or remove calls inspect the new hash bucket, missing the element stranded in its original bucket.

beats.title: HashSet vs. LinkedHashSet

top.label: Standard HashSet
points: Iterates in arbitrary hash bucket order
Slightly lower memory footprint per item

bottom.label: LinkedHashSet

beats.narration: Standard HashSet iteration order is arbitrary because it depends on bucket distribution. If you need constant time lookup combined with deterministic insertion order, use LinkedHashSet, which maintains a doubly-linked chain across entries.

beats.title: Set Internals Locked In
takeaways: HashSet delegates to HashMap with a dummy value
Never mutate hashCode fields while in a Set
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): TreeSet ordering traps & silent duplicate deletions →
beats.narration: That is how hash sets manage uniqueness and ordering. Next in Part 4, we examine TreeSet and uncover how bad comparators silently delete valid domain records.

beats.headline: TreeSet ignores the equals method entirely.
beats.subline: An incomplete comparator will silently discard valid business records.
beats.narration: TreeSet completely ignores the equals method when checking for duplicate entries, meaning an incomplete comparator will silently discard valid business records without throwing errors.

beats.title: HashSet vs. TreeSet Duplication Logic

top.label: HashSet Duplication
top.code:
// Uses hashCode bucket + equals() match
Set<Order> set = new HashSet<>();

bottom.label: TreeSet Duplication
points: Compares only via Comparator or Comparable
If compare returns 0, second item is discarded!

beats.narration: HashSet checks duplicate elements using hashCode and equals. TreeSet uses a Red-Black tree and determines uniqueness strictly when compareTo or compare returns zero. If two distinct items share the same price, TreeSet drops the second one.

beats.title: Chaining Unique Tie-Breakers

steps.explanation: Sorts orders primarily by double price ascending.
Chaining orderId guarantees distinct orders never evaluate to zero.

beats.narration: To keep TreeSet consistent with equals, always chain a unique secondary field with thenComparing. Here, comparing price first and then orderId guarantees two distinct orders never evaluate to zero, protecting your collection from silent data loss.

beats.title: NavigableSet Range Queries

steps.explanation: Fetches minimum and maximum elements in logarithmic O(log n) time.
Ceiling returns least element >= key; floor returns greatest <= key.

beats.narration: TreeSet implements NavigableSet, enabling logarithmic range lookups. Calling first or last returns tree boundaries, while ceiling and floor instantly locate nearest matching values relative to any given search key.

beats.title: TreeSet Mechanics Mastered
takeaways: Chain thenComparing to avoid silent element loss
NavigableSet provides O(log n) range queries

beats.headline: A single-threaded loop can crash with ConcurrentModificationException.
beats.subline: Mutating a collection during for-each iteration triggers modCount checks.
beats.narration: Modifying a collection inside an enhanced for-each loop triggers a ConcurrentModificationException instantly, even when running on a single isolated thread.

beats.title: Safe Collection Removals

steps.explanation: Updates expectedModCount synchronously to keep iteration safe.
Performs bulk removal in linear time without multi-pass array shifts.

beats.narration: Collections track internal modifications using a modCount counter. Direct list removal during iteration causes modCount mismatch. To remove safely, call Iterator dot remove or use modern removeIf, which keeps counters in sync.

beats.title: Java 21 Sequenced Collections (JEP 431)

steps.explanation: getFirst() and getLast() operate uniformly across Lists, Sets, and Deques.
reversed() returns a reverse view with zero memory allocations.

beats.narration: Java 21 introduced SequencedCollection to standardize ordered operations. Methods like getFirst and getLast provide uniform access across lists and sets, while reversed returns a zero-allocation reverse view.
